system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2167-05-27 17:18:00 to 2167-05-30 16:41:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a 58-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia s/p allogeneic cord blood transplant and chronic graft-versus-host disease, was admitted for worsening joint pain, fatigue, and nausea. His pain had increased after reducing OxyContin and stopping Plaquenil due to nausea. Labs showed elevated CRP indicating inflammation, but no infection. Prednisone was increased to 20mg daily, OxyContin was resumed twice daily, and morphine was provided for breakthrough pain due to oxycodone shortage. He developed transient hypotension attributed to narcotics, which resolved with dose adjustment. Podiatry removed bilateral ingrown toenails; a minor infection was treated with Keflex and topical antibiotic. Constipation and GERD were managed with senna/Colace and twice-daily esomeprazole. His pain, fatigue, and nausea improved, and he was discharged home in good condition with updated medications and follow-up plans.
problems: Pain in joint, other specified sites
Acute myeloid leukemia, without mention of having achieved remission

#Syncope: Patient had syncopal episode the day of admission, 
where he was unresponsive for ~1 minute while lying flat. 
Unclear etiology, possible due to orthostatic hypotension (noted 
to have orthostatic physiology in the ICU and on the floor) vs 
arrythmia vs seizure activity. Of note, (per wife), patient has 
had many of these episodes recently ___ years, ___ episodes per 
week). Patient denied any heralding symptoms and was not 
post-ictal afterwards, but was noted to have a resting tremor in 
the MICU. His history of tremor is not consistent wtih seizure 
activity. It appears to be an intention tremor that gets worse 
when holding on to objects and is low in amplitude while high in 
frequency, bilateral and not associated with change in 
consciousness or incontinence.  

Noted to be hyperkalemic during the code, given amp D50 and 10 U 
insulin ___ and kayexalate in the ICU, with drop in 
potassium down to 4.0 on discharge.   Neurology consulted on 
patient who recommended EEG and possible midodrine or fluorinef 
support. Held patient's lisinopril, but continued him on his 
carvedilol 12.5 mg PO BID as this was recently decreased in the 
setting of light headedness/dizziness by his cardiologist on 
___, although informed him not to take the medication if he had 
any pre-syncopal symptoms. Medication can be decreased at the 
discretion of his cardiologist. Patient had no further syncopal 
episodes or events on telemetry in the ICU or on the floor. 
Neurology was consulted who recommended an EEG, possible blood 
pressure support with midodrine or fluorinef, at the discretion 
of the patient's outpatient oncologist and nephrologist. Was 
noted to not have any telemetry events or syncopal events while 
ambulating, with appropriate increase in pulse and blood 
pressure. and requested to be discharged with outpatient syncope 
work-up. Outpatient TTE, EEG, carotid U/S, and holter monitering 
were arranged prior to discharge.  

#Acute on chronic renal failure: Noted to have mildly elevated 
Cre to 2.3 in clinic the day of admission. Creatine has 
fluctuated over the past ___ years, with several episodes of 
acute renal failure while hospitalized. Followed by nephrology 
as an outpatient. Per outpatient notes, etiology of CKD thought 
to be ___ ATN that has not resolved, medication effect in the 
setting of bactrim, voriconazole, lisinopril, or AIN. Less 
likely due to AML infiltration of kidneys (very rare) or 
chemotherapy. Unlikely progressive glomerular disease given 
patient only has scant proteinuria. Patient has refused renal 
biopsy in the past. Baseline Cre has been 1.4-2.0 over the past 
few months.  Lisinopril was held. Cellcept was decreased to 
___ as GFR was ~30. Oral fluid intake encouraged. Renal 
failure resolved to baseline creatinine (1.9) on discharge. 
Renal did not have chance to formally consult on patient since 
he requested discharge, but stated informally that they had no 
further recommendations as an inpatient since he was refusing 
renal biopsy, and he could be accommodated very soon in ___ 
clinic with his current outpatient nephrologist. 
 
#Congestive Heart Failure: Euvolemic to mildly hypervolemic on 
exam. Requested TTE as outpatient. Continued home meds including 
aspirin, beta-blocker. Held ACEI due to hyperkalemia. 

#AML: allo SCT +519 days. counts stable. continued prophylactic

#Syncope: Patient had syncopal episode the day of admission, 
where he was unresponsive for ~1 minute while lying flat. 
Unclear etiology, possible due to orthostatic hypotension (noted 
to have orthostatic physiology in the ICU and on the floor) vs 
arrythmia vs seizure activity. Of note, (per wife), patient has 
had many of these episodes recently ___ years, ___ episodes per 
week). Patient denied any heralding symptoms and was not 
post-ictal afterwards, but was noted to have a resting tremor in 
the MICU. His history of tremor is not consistent wtih seizure 
activity. It appears to be an intention tremor that gets worse 
when holding on to objects and is low in amplitude while high in 
frequency, bilateral and not associated with change in 
consciousness or incontinence.  

Noted to be hyperkalemic during the code, given amp D50 and 10 U 
insulin ___ and kayexalate in the ICU, with drop in 
potassium down to 4.0 on discharge.   Neurology consulted on 
patient who recommended EEG and possible midodrine or fluorinef 
support. Held patient's lisinopril, but continued him on his 
carvedilol 12.5 mg PO BID as this was recently decreased in the 
setting of light headedness/dizziness by his cardiologist on 
___, although informed him not to take the medication if he had 
any pre-syncopal symptoms. Medication can be decreased at the

Neurology was consulted who recommended an EEG, possible blood 
pressure support with midodrine or fluorinef, at the discretion

ambulating, with appropriate increase in pulse and blood

work-up. Outpatient TTE, EEG, carotid U/S, and holter monitering

acute renal failure while hospitalized. Followed by nephrology

to be ___ ATN that has not resolved, medication effect in the 
setting of bactrim, voriconazole, lisinopril, or AIN. Less 
likely due to AML infiltration of kidneys (very rare) or 
chemotherapy. Unlikely progressive glomerular disease given 
patient only has scant proteinuria. Patient has refused renal 
biopsy in the past. Baseline Cre has been 1.4-2.0 over the past 
few months.  Lisinopril was held. Cellcept was decreased to 
___ as GFR was ~30. Oral fluid intake encouraged. Renal

Renal did not have chance to formally consult on patient since

#Congestive Heart Failure: Euvolemic to mildly hypervolemic on

#AML: allo SCT +519 days. counts stable. continued prophylactic

#Epigastric discomfort: Gastritis, likely in setting of

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you came in from clinic today because your kidney numbers were high and you've been feeling unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. My creatinine was 2.3, and I’ve been more tired than usual. I also had some trouble swallowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And I understand you had a brief episode when you arrived—became unresponsive for a moment. Do you remember that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I just remember lying down and then people around me. My wife said my eyes were closed and I didn’t respond.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We called a code because your potassium was high and your EKG showed peaked T waves. We gave you insulin and dextrose to bring it down quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know it was that serious. Is my potassium okay now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was 5.5 when you arrived, which is high. We treated it, and it’s coming down. We’ll keep monitoring it. We also gave you kayexalate to help your body get rid of extra potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But why did I pass out? That’s never happened before like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not entirely clear. It could be related to the high potassium, or maybe a blood pressure drop. Your wife mentioned you’ve had brief episodes like this before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, yes—maybe once or twice a week for the past few months. Just seconds, I’m told. I don’t remember them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ve consulted neurology. They think it’s worth checking with an EEG and maybe a Holter monitor to rule out seizures or heart rhythm issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An EEG? Like for seizures? But I don’t jerk or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You don’t have the typical signs, but brief lapses in awareness can still be neurological. We also noticed a tremor in your hands when you’re holding things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s been there for years. Gets worse when I try to hold a cup or write. My wife calls it a shaky hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like an intention tremor. It’s not typical for seizures, which is reassuring. But we still want to evaluate the episodes of unresponsiveness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can we do those tests later? I’m feeling better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can arrange them as outpatient tests. We’ve scheduled an EEG, a Holter monitor, carotid ultrasound, and an echocardiogram.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds okay. What about my kidneys? That’s why I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your baseline creatinine has been between 1.4 and 2.0. It went up to 2.3, so we’re calling this acute on chronic kidney injury. We think it’s partly due to your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like which ones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lisinopril, voriconazole, and Bactrim can all affect the kidneys. We’ve held your lisinopril for now because it can also raise potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that for years. Should I stop it for good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. We’ll discuss restarting it with your nephrologist. We’ve also reduced your Cellcept dose because your kidney function is reduced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my stomach’s been bothering me—burning, especially after taking prednisone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, prednisone can cause gastritis. You said Nexium hasn’t helped for the past three months?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. I still wake up with acid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to Protonix, which might work better. You may need prior authorization, but your oncologist can help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my breathing? I’ve felt a bit swollen in the legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have mild swelling, and your exam shows you’re a bit fluid overloaded. But your chest X-ray shows no pneumonia or heart failure. We’ll keep you on your furosemide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to end up on oxygen again like with BOOP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching closely. Your heart enzymes and ABG were normal, so no sign of heart damage or breathing trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. Your potassium is now 4.0, and creatinine is down to 1.9—back to your baseline. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. No more episodes either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And telemetry showed no arrhythmias. The head CT was normal—no bleeding or stroke. Just some sinus inflammation, which we already knew about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you’re feeling well. We’ll discharge you tomorrow. Just need to make sure you’re stable through the night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are stable. You’ve had no syncopal episodes, and your vitals are good. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your meds as listed, except hold lisinopril. Take Protonix for your stomach. And watch for fever, fainting, chest pain—come back if any of those happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the follow-up tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All scheduled—EEG, Holter, echo, carotid ultrasound. Your oncologist and nephrologist will get the results and guide next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your records are sent to your team. Take care, and see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. You’re afebrile, blood pressure stable, no dizziness. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the care. I’ll follow up on those tests right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And call us if anything changes. Your wife has the discharge instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’s got everything. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. Stay hydrated and keep up with your appointments.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a 58-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia s/p allogeneic cord blood transplant and chronic graft-versus-host disease, was admitted for acute on chronic renal failure and hyperkalemia. He experienced a brief syncopal episode upon arrival, prompting a code blue due to severe hyperkalemia, which was treated with insulin, dextrose, and kayexalate. His potassium normalized, and renal function returned to baseline. The syncopal episodes, both recent and historical, were evaluated with neurology input, leading to outpatient EEG, Holter monitor, carotid ultrasound, and echocardiogram referrals. Lisinopril was held due to hyperkalemia, Cellcept was dose-reduced, and Protonix was started for refractory gastritis. He remained stable without further events and was discharged home in good condition with follow-up arranged.
